# Diamonds dataset 
Categorical variable: cut,
Continuous variable: carat

```{r}
diamonds <- read.csv("diamonds 2.csv")
diamonds
```


# Task 1: Describe a categorical variable

```{r}
diamonds %>%
  ggplot() +
    geom_bar(mapping = aes(y = cut), width = 0.6)
```

```{r}
diamonds %>%
  group_by(cut) %>%
  summarize(count = n())
```

In our dataset, the "fair" cut has the lowest count, at 1610. In our dataset, the count for the "ideal" cut is the highest, at 21551. In our dataset, this would make sense since people tend to desire more "ideal" cut diamonds as opposed to "fair" cut diamonds. 

# Task 2: Describe a continuous variable

```{r}
diamonds %>%
  ggplot() + 
  geom_histogram(mapping = aes(x=carat))
```

```{r}
diamonds %>%
summarise(
Min = min(carat), 
Q1 = quantile(carat, probs = 0.25), 
Median = median(carat),
Q3 = quantile(carat, probs = 0.75), 
Max = max(carat)
)
```

The histogram has a left skew since all the carat values are shifted to the left. As a result, I decided to use a five-number summary instead of mean and standard deviation since this was not a normal distribution with an expected bell-shaped curve. Through the five-number summary, I was able to see that the range of data values in our dataset was very large, from 0.2 to 5.01, and the Q1 and Q3 values are almost exactly halfway between the minimum and median and the max and median, respectfully. This shows that in this dataset, a larger carat diamond is more sparse and is less abundant than a smaller carat diamond. 

# Task 3: Relationship between two variables

```{r}
diamonds %>%
  ggplot() + 
  geom_point(mapping = aes(x=carat, y=price))
```

In our dataset, as the carat size increases, the price of the diamond increases. This would be a positive correlation between the carat size and the diamond's price. There are some fluctuating prices that appear at certain, specific carat sizes, such as 1.5 carat diamonds. This could be because of the new popularity of lab-grown diamonds, where there are an abundance of carats at different prices since jewelers and people who make diamonds have a lot of diamonds that they can price at different prices depending on the store. This also occurs in this dataset at 2 carats and 3 carats, indicating these carats might be the most popular for individuals buying the diamonds in this dataset. We can also see that in this dataset, it is much less common to see super large and super expensive carats, and more common to see smaller, less expensive diamonds. This makes sense since there are fewer "premium" cut diamonds, which tend to be more expensive. This also makes sense since many people would prefer a more affordable diamond that allows more people to purchase it.
